chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd from 'Asim from 'Anbasah ibn Mus'abb said:

I saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Mina walking and riding. I told myself that I would ask him when I entered upon him, but he initiated the conversation with me, saying: 'Indeed, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon them both) used to leave his house on foot when he threw the Jamarat. My house today is more spacious than his house, so I ride until I reach his house.' Then when I reached his house, I walked until I threw the Jamarat.
And there is no objection if the Jamarat is thrown on behalf of the sick, the one with a full stomach (or indigestion), the unconscious, the child, and those similar to them.

key_terms.وَالْمَبْطُونِ: And the one with a full stomach/indigestion

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to throw the Jamarat on behalf of someone who is sick or a child?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the flexibility (*rukhas*) in Hajj rituals, where Imam al-Sajjad (AS) prioritized ease over rigid adherence to walking, demonstrating that the choice between riding and walking is a matter of personal capacity rather than strict obligation. The narration further extends this leniency to those unable to perform the act themselves, such as the sick, unconscious, or young children, allowing for proxy throwing (*ramy 'anhum*). This reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle of removing hardship (*raf' al-haraj*) in acts of worship.
